bib.title: Budget-Aware Tool Use Enables Effective Agent Scaling

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Budget-Aware Tool Use Enables Effective Agent Scaling", Tengxiao Liu, Zifeng Wang, Jin Miao, I-Hung Hsu, Jun Yan, Jiefeng Chen, Rujun Han, Fangyuan Xu, Yanfei Chen, Ke Jiang, Samira Daruki, Yi Liang, William Yang Wang, Tomas Pfister, Chen-Yu Lee (UCSB, Google Cloud AI Research, Google DeepMind, NYU). arXiv:2511.17006v2, preprint, "17 Aug 2026" on the stamp (v2). Year in the file name is 2025.

COVERAGE: All 32 of 32 pages, 96,109 of 96,109 chars. Main text, appendices A-G, algorithm and prompts were read. The reference list was only skimmed. Prompts D.2 to D.4 were not read line by line, only D.1's budget section. Figure images were not viewed. I did not read the whole target note, only its first ~3,000 chars. Its frontmatter lists no Liu/arXiv 2511.17006 source.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: A plain ReAct agent does not use extra tool budget. Accuracy plateaus and tool-call counts stay almost flat as the cap rises. The agent stops early because it thinks it has an answer, even though the context is not full.
  number: Gemini-2.5-Pro on BrowseComp averages 13.77 search calls at budget 30 and 14.24 at budget 100. Accuracy is 10.5% at 30 and 12.6% at 100.
  setup: ReAct, search and browse tools, BrowseComp, per-tool budget.
  quote: "Gemini-2.5-Pro with ReAct uses nearly identical numbers of tool calls whether the budget is 30 or 100 (13.77 vs. 14.24 search calls), and its accuracy barely changes."
  where: App. E.1 (p. 28); Table 5 (p. 19); Fig. 3 (p. 6)
- claim: The Budget Tracker is a plug-in that injects the remaining and used budget per tool into the context every turn. It gives the same accuracy at a tenth of the cap, with lower cost.
  number: Budget 10 with tracker gets 12.8% against ReAct at budget 100 with 12.6%. It makes 40.4% fewer search calls, 19.9% fewer browse calls and costs 31.3% less.
  setup: Gemini-2.5-Pro, BrowseComp, ReAct, no training, average cost per question 6.8¢ against 9.9¢.
  quote: "Budget Tracker achieves comparable accuracy with less budget (10 vs. 100), while using 40.4% fewer search calls, 19.9% fewer browse calls, and reducing overall cost by 31.3%."
  where: Sec. 3.3 (p. 5-6); Table 2
- claim: Tracker gives a consistent accuracy gain at equal budget (100 per tool), across models and benchmarks.
  number: Gemini-2.5-Pro BrowseComp 12.6 to 14.6, BrowseComp-ZH 31.5 to 32.9, HLE-Search 20.5 to 21.8. Claude-Sonnet-4 BrowseComp 12.2 to 14.0, HLE-Search 20.5 to 23.0. Gemini-2.5-Flash BrowseComp 9.7 to 10.7.
  setup: Mean of 3 runs. The gains are small, around 1 to 3 points, and the ± values are about 0.2 to 2.3.
  quote: "Across different models, adding the tracker consistently improves accuracy on all the datasets."
  where: Table 1 (p. 6)
- claim: The full BATS framework (budget-aware planning, then verification with SUCCESS, CONTINUE or PIVOT) roughly doubles ReAct accuracy on BrowseComp with no training, at a 100-per-tool budget.
  number: Gemini-2.5-Pro BrowseComp 24.6 against ReAct 12.6. BrowseComp-ZH 46.0 against 31.5. HLE-Search 27.0 against 20.5. Claude-Sonnet-4 BrowseComp 19.1 against 12.2. SLIM, a summarizing baseline, scores 13.4 for Gemini-2.5-Pro.
  setup: Budget 100 per tool. OpenAI Deep Research (trained) scores 51.5 on BrowseComp, so BATS is far below it.
  quote: "BATS consistently achieves better results than baselines, obtaining 24.6% on BrowseComp, 46.0% on BrowseComp-ZH and 27.0% on HLE-Search using Gemini-2.5-Pro."
  where: Table 3 (p. 10); Sec. 5.2
- claim: Budget awareness also helps outside search. On tau2-bench retail it improves reliability. On SWE-bench Verified with a coding agent, resolve rate jumps at the same budget.
  number: tau2 (Gemini-2.5-Flash): at budget 10, Avg@4 rose 47.8 to 55.5 and Pass^4 21.9 to 27.2. The tracker at budget 10 beat the baseline at budget 50 on Pass^4 (27.2 vs 26.3) with 5.38 vs 6.59 tool calls. SWE-bench Verified (Gemini-3-Flash-Preview, mini-swe-agent, 500 tasks): at budget 50, 55.4% against 36.8%, with 45.7 vs 46.0 tool calls and 18.88¢ vs 18.50¢. The tracker at 50 also beat the baseline at 60 (55.4 vs 53.2).
  setup: Global tool-call budget, not per-tool. Baseline at budget 70 reached 63.0 against tracker 55.1 at 70, so the tracker does not win at every budget.
  quote: "Budget Tracker increases the resolve rate by 18.6 percentage points (55.4% vs. 36.8%) while using a similar number of tool calls (45.7 vs. 46.0)"
  where: App. C.2-C.3 (p. 19-21); Tables 6-7
- claim: The ablation shows verification matters more than planning on BrowseComp. Retries after a first verified answer add 5.9 points.
  number: BATS with early stop scores 18.7. Without planning 17.0, without verification 15.4, without both 14.6. Full BATS is 24.6.
  setup: Gemini-2.5-Pro, budget 100 per tool. BrowseComp-ZH and HLE-Search ablation results are noisier.
  quote: "removing the verification module causes a more significant drop on BrowseComp (from 18.7% to 15.4%)."
  where: Table 4 (p. 10); App. E.4
- claim: Budget awareness works by changing strategy (broad when rich, precise when poor) and by allocating more calls to browse. It does not work by spending more.
  number: browse-to-search ratio 9.6% (ReAct) against 12.9% (tracker). Early stop on BrowseComp-ZH: ReAct tops out at 30.7% for every budget of 30 or more, while BATS goes from 29.8% (budget 3) to 37.4% (budget 200).
  setup: Gemini-2.5-Pro. Based on two case studies (Figs. 15-16) and the Table 2 ratio.
  quote: "ReAct baseline ... reaches a performance plateau early, with accuracy capped at 30.7% for all budgets of 30 and above."
  where: App. C.6 (p. 22), E.2-E.3 (p. 28-29)
- claim: BATS beats parallel majority voting on cost for the same accuracy.
  number: over 37% accuracy at about $0.23, against over $0.50 for parallel voting.
  setup: Early-stop BATS, BrowseComp-ZH, Gemini-2.5-Pro.
  quote: "BATS reaches over 37% accuracy for approximately $0.23, while the parallel baseline requires more than double that cost (over $0.50) to achieve a comparable result."
  where: App. C.6 (p. 23)
- claim: The paper defines a unified cost metric that adds token cost to tool cost. Tool calls are priced at a flat rate.
  number: $0.001 per call.
  setup: Search and browse calls are priced at an average derived from post hoc statistics. Tokens are billed at provider rates, with cache hits counted.
  quote: "we've established a unified rate of $0.001 per invocation for both search API calls and web browsing actions."
  where: App. A.1 (p. 18); Eq. 2
- claim: Hard cap vs soft signal. The budget is a hard constraint, enforced per tool per question, and BATS terminates when any one budget is exhausted. A tool-call budget is chosen over a token budget because a token budget is hard to set ahead of time.
  number: none
  quote: "the constraint ensures that for any given question, the number of realized calls for each tool never exceeds its allocated budget."
  where: Eq. 1, Sec. 2.1 (p. 3)
  setup: The enforcement mechanism is not described beyond "the process stops when any budget is exhausted". The paper does not say whether the cap sits outside the model, though the algorithm loop does check it.
- claim: Context management used in the experiments.
  number: webpage truncated to 150,000 chars. Only the latest tool response is kept. BATS replaces the old trace with a summary after K=10 iterations. Dropping old tool outputs gives similar accuracy (24.6 vs 24.3) and cost $1.1 vs $1.2.
  setup: Gemini-2.5-Pro, BrowseComp.
  quote: "At every iteration, we discard tool outputs from previous steps and retain only the most recent tool response"
  where: App. A.2 (p. 18); Table 9 (p. 23)

LIMITS
- The authors list four limits: only tool-call budgets (no joint token, latency or tool limits), high compute cost that prevents repeated runs and hyperparameter search, no study of how an agent should allocate its budget, and only simple context management.
- The authors say that "models often underestimate their actual resource consumption" (App. G, p. 31).
- Most results come from one model family (Gemini-2.5, plus Claude-Sonnet-4 in main tables) and three web-search benchmarks.
- The tau2 and SWE-bench results are appendix-only. SWE-bench uses Gemini-3-Flash-Preview, a different model from the main study. At budget 70 the tracker (55.1) is below the baseline (63.0).
- Gains for Budget Tracker alone in Table 1 are 1 to 3 points on single-digit to low-30s accuracies. The tool-call budgets are small relative to the 50 to 150 range studied.
- The budget is a prompt-visible signal, so it relies on the model's cooperation. The paper reports no tests of an agent that ignores or tampers with the budget, nor adversarial or safety use.
- Over-budget handling: ReAct hits the cap on 42.81% of queries for Flash at budget 30 (Table 5). What happens at cap (forced answer from progress so far) is described only in the early-stop setting (App. C.6).
- Its absolute accuracies are far below the trained OpenAI Deep Research (51.5% on BrowseComp).
- The v2 date (Aug 2026) and Gemini-2.5-era models may have dated.

BUILDS ON: ReAct (Yao et al., 2023); budget forcing (Muennighoff et al., 2025); test-time scaling (Snell et al., 2024; Brown et al., 2024 "Large language monkeys"; Wang et al., 2023 self-consistency); Shen et al. (2025) for test-time interaction scaling; SLIM (Yen et al., 2025) as a baseline; MiroThinker (Team et al., 2025b); BrowseComp (Wei et al., 2025); tau2-bench (Barres et al., 2025); prompts from Jin et al. (2025) Search-R1 and Li et al. (2025b); AgentTTS (Wang et al., 2025a). Also cites Anthropic (2025) "Effective context engineering for AI agents".

CODE
Budget block, appended after each tool response (Sec. 3.1, p. 5):
<budget>
Tool_i Budget Used: ##, Tool_i Budget Remaining: ##
Make the best use of the available resources.
</budget>
Regime policy in the first-turn prompt (D.1, p. 24): "HIGH Budget (>=70% remaining) Search: 3-5 diverse queries in one batch. Browse: up to 2-3 high-value URLs. Goal: Broad exploration, build context fast." and "MEDIUM Budget (30%-70%) Search: 2-3 precise, refined queries per cycle. Browse: 1-2 URLs that close key knowledge gaps." (a LOW regime follows; I did not read its text.)
Eq. 1: max_pi Acc_b(pi) s.t. c_i(x;pi) <= b_i for all i and every x. Eq. 2: C_unified = c_token + sum_i c_i * P_i.
Algorithm 1 (p. 32): while u_i < b_i for all i: inject b-u via the tracker, reason, and update the tree plan. Either call a tool (u_i += 1) or propose an answer and verify it. SUCCESS adds it to the verified set A and starts a new attempt. CONTINUE compresses and goes on. PIVOT summarizes, resets the context and abandons the direction. When the loop ends, the LLM judge picks from A, falling back to the last candidate.

FIGURES
- Fig. 1 (p. 2): Budget Tracker as a plug-in on ReAct (top) and BATS (bottom). Shows where the tracker sits in the loop.
- Fig. 2 (p. 4): The tracker view the agent sees each turn (Query Budget 50/50, URL Budget 50/50).
- Fig. 3 (p. 6): Gemini-2.5-Pro, BrowseComp. ReAct saturates at budget 100 while the tracker keeps climbing. This is the key plot for the ceiling claim.
- Fig. 4-5 (p. 7): Sequential and parallel scaling, where the Pareto frontier shifts left and up.
- Fig. 6 (p. 7): BATS overview with the Continue/Pivot/Success flow.
- Fig. 7 (p. 9): Accuracy vs tool calls and vs cost, BATS against parallel majority vote.
- Fig. 9 (p. 22): Early-stop bars (tool use) plus accuracy line. ReAct flat, BATS scaling.
- Figs. 15-17 (p. 30): Cases of high-budget, low-budget and PIVOT behaviour.

PROBLEMS: No extraction faults beyond garbled table layouts (for example the "5063.2 36.0" row is 50 / 63.2 / 36.0, and the SWE-bench "7070.055.1" row is 70 / 70.0 / 55.1). No embedded instructions found. The first Bash call's persisted output was truncated to 40k chars, so I re-extracted the whole text. The cached text is at /tmp/liu_full.txt. Fit with the target note: it concerns cost ceilings that sit outside what the agent can edit. This paper treats the budget as an in-context signal plus a hard cap, and offers no evidence on sandbox escape or permissions. It sharpens the "cost ceilings" part only, and the claim that agents don't use their headroom is the useful part.
